source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 27% of people in Israel were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%.
37.9% of health spending in Israel was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
4% of hospital care costs in Israel were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
44% of outpatient medical care costs in Israel were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
99% of dental care costs in Israel were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
47% of pharmaceutical costs in Israel were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.
Israel and the Netherlands had the largest supplementary health insurance market (over 80% of the population).
Financial coverage for outpatient care was under 60% in Latvia, Israel, Portugal, Italy and Korea.

Teleconsultations comprised over 25% of all doctor consultations in Denmark, Estonia, Israel, Portugal and Sweden, but remained very low in Chile, Germany, Greece and Korea (see the section on “Data and digital” in Chapter 9 for trends in teleconsultations).

Across all staff types, positive perceptions on staffing and work pace are highest in Poland, Israel, Colombia, the United States and Latvia (50% or more with positive perceptions across different types).
Australia and Israel also exhibit relatively high healthcare prices.
Government transfers fund two-thirds of the social health insurance system in Chile, and over 50% of all their revenues in Hungary and Israel.
Taken together, in 2023, spending on outpatient care services accounted for around 45% of all health spending in Israel, Portugal and Estonia compared to an OECD average of 33%.
